newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - British utility regulators put to the test.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - British utility regulators put to the test.

text.p: Gas and electricity reviews dragged Britain's utilities back into the spotlight on Thursday, but analysts said despite British Gas's decision to reject price cut proposals, the regulatory system was not in tatters.

British Gas scorned regulator Clare Spottiswoode's plans, that would wipe two billion pounds ($3.1 billion) off the cash flow from the company's Transo pipeline business over five years, as "unjustified and unworkable".
Analysts say the cuts could slash dividends.

The battle between industry regulators and the privatised utilities has already seen Northern Ireland Electricity (NIE) demand a Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC) inquiry in August, rejecting electricity regulator Offer's stringent price cut proposals as "outlandish".

But analysts say the regulatory system, which differs from the American one by curbing the prices firms charge consumers rather than profits -- thus safeguarding efficiency incentives -- has not failed despite the two latest MMC referrals.

Experts do not think the National Grid, which owns and operates the high-voltage power transmission system and saw Offer's final pricing plans on Thursday, will risk the uncertaintly of a lengthy MMC referral.

"With Gas, you're looking at a massive dividend cut -- so anything is worth a try -- whereas with the Grid, it's just about the rate of the increase of dividend growth," noted one analyst, who declined to be named.
"As for NIE...they may have been playing the political card. They are the largest employer in the province."
The Grid, the last utility to see its watchdog's pricing plans unveiled this century, will see revenues cut by around one billion pounds over four years.
"All the regulators are moving in exactly the same direction, which is to tighten the regulatory regime, cut prices, reduce returns," said Irene Himona, analyst at brokers SG Strauss Turnbull.

Continental European countries such as Italy and Spain are looking at Britain's system, under which prices that can be charged are linked to inflation, to see whether such a system would be viable as they begin privatising their utilities.

"A number of governments and regulators are looking at the UK's example of regulation and believe it has been instrumental in bringing down the price of electricity, for example, to the consumer," said Andy Stone, utilities analyst at brokers Daiwa.
But analysts are already predicting an end to the last, harsh round of regulatory reviews. Utilities are mostly more efficient now and have less room to cut costs and jobs.

"This form of regulation has been so successful -- it has shown there are some massive efficiencies," said one analyst. "Now is the time to give them back to customers. But in future you wouldn't expect these big adjustments," an analyst said.
About a third of jobs have been shed across the former state utilities since they were privatised.

British utility regulators, especially those governing the lucrative water and electricity distribution sectors, have been derided because of the perceived lenience of past reviews that have sent shares surging in relieved disbelief.
Headlines such as "Like water off a duck's back" greeted the reviews in August 1994.

But share analysts have become wary of regulators since bearded Offer chief Stephen Littlechild was last year so embarrassed by the largesse of companies' bid defence packages amid a wave of takeovers for electricity firms that he suddenly reopened a price review.
Headlines changed tack. One read: "Man with beard casts thunderbolt" as shares plunged. Utility watchdogs had started to show their teeth.
